newsitem.title: FRANCE: France seeks EU help to rein in Euro parliament.
newsitem.headline: France seeks EU help to rein in Euro parliament.

text.p: France on Thursday sought help from the European Union to rein in the European Parliament after condemning the legislature for urging Paris to withdraw a controversial immigration bill.

Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, extending a bitter clash with the Strasbourg-based assembly, said he would ask foreign ministers from the other 14 nations "to reflect on the European Parliament's exceeding its responsibilities".
The parliament "must fully exercise its responsibilities, but only those, and not interfere in the French process, in the legislative process. To each his job," de Charette told France Inter radio.

The dispute illustrates scepticism in France about a drive by the 626-member parliament, the EU's only directly-elected body, to gain wider powers at the expense of national parliaments under a current review of EU institutions.

The president of the European Parliament, Jose-Maria Gil-Robles, cancelled a meeting with de Charette on Wednesday after the French minister branded the legislature "not yet a parliament worthy of the name".

De Charette, calling himself a "convinced European", said he was not withdrawing any of his criticisms. By contrast, Gil-Robles, a Spanish conservative, played down the incident on Wednesday and said he saw no point in prolonging the row.

The European Parliament narrowly adopted a motion last week urging the centre-right French government to withdraw its bill aimed at further tightening laws on illegal immigration that would allow stricter monitoring of legal third world visitors.

The National Assembly was holding a third day of stormy debate on the bill on Thursday and the centre-right coalition, which has a four-fifths majority, is hoping for a final vote to approve it later in the day.

De Charette also said it was quite possible France would bring up the issue of the European Parliament's powers as part of a review of EU institutions at a current inter-governmental conference (IGC).
The parliament wants wider powers, including the right to elect the president of the European Commission, a bigger say in law-making and shaping a common EU defence policy.
Under current rules, the parliament can sack the European Commission and reject the EU central budget. It can also reject some laws and must approve association accords with non-member states.
France and Britain have been opposed to extending its powers while Germany is in favour. Even so, France has widely funded the parliament and pushed to anchor it in Strasbourg rather than Brussels.

President Jacques Chirac began the French protests on Tuesday, calling the parliament vote "unacceptable". The motion, adopted by 106-101 votes last Thursday, was part of a resolution "on racism, xenophobia and the extreme right".

Former Socialist prime minister Laurent Fabius, the party's floor leader in the National Assembly, agreed that "French laws are voted in the National Assembly" but said the vote was symptomatic of unease in Europe about xenophobia.
"This law is inopportune," he told RTL radio.

De Charette recalled that when Chirac visited the European parliament in July 1995, leftist members of the parliament jeered him and waved posters showing mushroom clouds to protest at France's decision to resume nuclear testing.
"That would not be possible in the French parliament. If that happened, the ushers would take away the banners," he said.
